strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning multiple bitrates (high/low), clean and noisy conditions, and a wide range of recent SOTA baselines (X-Codec, X-Codec2, XY-Tokenizer, Mimi, BigCodec, SemantiCodec, SpeechTokenizer, MagiCodec, TS3-Codec, etc.), giving good coverage of the competitive landscape.

The dual-stream design (fully separate semantic and acoustic quantization, rather than the fused 'X-shaped' injection used in prior work) is a reasonably motivated architectural contribution, and the paper provides clear ablations (Table 4) isolating the effect of semantic and speaker auxiliary losses.

The disentanglement analysis (Section 5.4, Table 5, Fig. 3-4) is a genuinely interesting contribution: quantitative (WER, SIM, MSIM) and qualitative (mel-spectrogram) evidence showing near-complete separation of linguistic content from speaker/timbre information, with a direct comparison against SemantiCodec and SpeechTokenizer that strengthens the disentanglement claim.

Strong quantitative results across reconstruction metrics (UTMOS, WER, SIM) at comparable bitrates, and semantic representation results on the ARCH benchmark that approach or exceed several SSL models, which is a notable finding for codec-based representations.
Reasonable reproducibility support: detailed training data composition (Appendix A), architecture and hyperparameter details (Appendix B), and a stated commitment to release code/checkpoints.
Additional robustness evaluation under noisy conditions (test-other) strengthens the practical relevance of the claims beyond clean benchmark performance.
weaknesses: The core architectural novelty is somewhat incremental: the main semantic stream simply reuses an existing frozen pretrained semantic tokenizer (Zeng et al., 2024b), so much of the semantic-representation improvement may stem from that strong pretrained component rather than from the 'dual-stream' architecture itself. No ablation isolates architecture vs. tokenizer choice (e.g., using the same frozen tokenizer inside an X-shaped fusion baseline) to cleanly attribute the gains.

Baselines are reproduced from official checkpoints trained on their own (often smaller or differently composed) datasets, while SAC is trained on a large curated 20k-hour bilingual corpus; this confounds comparisons and makes it hard to conclude that the architectural design (rather than training data scale/diversity) drives the reported gains.

All quality evaluation relies on automatic metrics (UTMOS, PESQ, STOI, WER, SIM); no human/subjective MOS evaluation is reported, which is a concern especially since SAC's UTMOS scores exceed ground-truth recordings, a result that could reflect predictor bias/over-smoothing rather than genuinely superior quality, and this is not critically discussed.

The semantic representation evaluation (ARCH) uses only linear probing with temporal average pooling over four fairly simple tasks; no evaluation of the codec tokens in actual downstream generative or understanding pipelines (e.g., training a speech LM or TTS system on SAC tokens) is provided, despite the motivation explicitly being SLM applications.
No statistical significance testing or repeated runs are reported; single-run point estimates are used throughout for both main results and ablations.

The paper's discussion of why the dual-stream design outperforms X-shaped fusion is largely qualitative/hypothesis-driven (e.g., 'we attribute this to...', 'we hypothesize...') rather than directly tested with additional controlled experiments.

strengths: The paper presents an extremely thorough empirical evaluation, covering high- and low-bitrate reconstruction, noisy-condition robustness, semantic representation (ARCH benchmark), downstream LLM-based TTS, disentanglement analysis (both quantitative SIM/MSIM and qualitative spectrogram visualization), subjective MOS testing, inference speed (RTF), training-data-scale ablation, and loss-component ablations — a level of comprehensiveness rarely seen and valuable for reproducibility and trust in the results.

The dual-stream design (fully separate, independently quantized semantic and acoustic tokens fused only at decoding) is a clean and well-motivated architectural choice that is clearly differentiated from prior 'X-shaped' fusion-before-quantization codecs (X-Codec, XY-Tokenizer) and from SemantiCodec, and the paper provides concrete empirical evidence (Table 5, Figure 3/4) that this design yields cleaner semantic/acoustic disentanglement than prior decoupled codecs.

Results are strong and consistent across many metrics and bitrates: near-ground-truth WER, higher-than-ground-truth UTMOS, competitive PESQ/STOI, and large gains in semantic probing (ARCH) approaching or exceeding several SSL models, with baselines reproduced from official checkpoints rather than only cited from other papers.

The downstream single-stage AR TTS experiment (100k-hour training) provides practically meaningful validation of the tokenizer's usefulness beyond reconstruction metrics, with clear improvements over strong AR baselines (Spark-TTS, Llasa) in WER/CER and UTMOS.

Extensive appendices proactively address likely reviewer concerns (data scale confounds, noisy robustness, RTF, ablation of auxiliary losses on semantic probing), reflecting good scientific diligence.
weaknesses: The core novelty is somewhat incremental: the semantic stream reuses an existing frozen pretrained tokenizer (Zeng et al. 2024b) rather than proposing a new semantic modeling method, and the acoustic stream follows standard DAC/Encodec-style design; the main contribution is largely architectural (keeping streams separate through decoding) plus two auxiliary supervision losses, which, while effective, is a comparatively modest technical advance relative to the breadth of claims made.

The code/model release link referenced in the abstract is missing/blank, and while training data and hyperparameters are described in detail, full reproducibility (e.g., exact pretrained semantic tokenizer checkpoint, exact training recipe replication) depends on artifacts not confirmed as available in the manuscript as presented.

Baseline models are trained on differing (often much smaller or differently distributed) datasets than SAC's 20k-hour bilingual corpus; although the paper acknowledges this and provides a small-data ablation (Appendix F), the main comparison tables still risk conflating architectural gains with data-scale/diversity advantages, especially for semantic representation and speaker similarity metrics.

Evaluation protocol inconsistencies: WER is computed with a HuBERT-based ASR in the main reconstruction tables but with Whisper-large-v3 in the disentanglement analysis (Table 5), and bitrates being compared as 'similar' are not always closely matched (e.g., 875 vs 800–1040 bps groupings), which could affect the fairness of head-to-head rankings shown in figures like Fig. 1.

The subjective MOS evaluation is based on a relatively small pool (20 listeners, 30 utterances) with no reported statistical significance/confidence intervals, limiting the strength of the naturalness claims beyond the automatic UTMOS metric.

Some tables omit certain strong baselines present in adjacent tables (e.g., BigCodec and X-Codec2 appear in the high-bitrate table but not the low-bitrate table), leaving gaps in the comparison landscape at matched bitrates.

The claimed 'first clean disentanglement between semantics and speaker identity' is an interesting but largely qualitative/anecdotal claim (based on one visualized example and MSIM/SIM on one test condition), and would benefit from broader quantitative validation (e.g., multiple speakers/languages, formal voice-conversion or anonymization task evaluation) before being emphasized as strongly as in the conclusion.

strengths: Extremely comprehensive empirical evaluation: reconstruction quality (STOI/PESQ/UTMOS/SIM/WER) at multiple bitrates, under both clean and noisy conditions, semantic representation via the ARCH benchmark, downstream LLM-based TTS, subjective MOS testing, training-data-scale ablation, and inference speed (RTF) — this breadth substantially strengthens the evidentiary base for the paper's claims.

The dual-stream design (frozen pretrained semantic tokenizer + separate acoustic codec, fused only at decoding) is a clean and well-motivated architectural choice that is clearly differentiated from prior 'X-shaped' fusion-before-quantization approaches (X-Codec, XY-Tokenizer) and from SemantiCodec's incomplete disentanglement.

Reported results are consistently strong and often near or above ground truth (e.g., UTMOS exceeding ground truth, WER close to ground truth) across both high- and low-bitrate regimes, and the same trends hold under noisy test conditions (Appendix C), supporting robustness of the claims.

The disentanglement analysis (Table 5, Fig. 3/4) provides compelling qualitative and quantitative evidence (near-total loss of speaker similarity in semantic-only reconstruction while retaining low WER, and vice versa for acoustic-only) that is a genuinely interesting and to some extent novel empirical finding with potential downstream relevance (voice conversion, anonymization, controllable TTS).

Reasonably detailed reproducibility information: training data composition (Table 6), hyperparameters, loss weights, and architecture parameter counts are provided in appendices, along with ablations isolating the effect of individual auxiliary losses.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the main contribution is largely a recombination of existing components (a frozen off-the-shelf semantic tokenizer from Zeng et al. 2024b, a DAC/Encodec-style acoustic codec, and ConvNeXt fusion), with the primary distinguishing choice being late (post-quantization) rather than pre-quantization fusion — a design already explored by SemantiCodec. Much of SAC's advantage over SemantiCodec plausibly stems from using a much stronger pretrained speech-specific semantic tokenizer rather than from the disentanglement idea itself.

Baseline comparisons are not fully consistent across tables: different subsets of competitor codecs appear in the high-bitrate vs. low-bitrate tables (e.g., Mimi, BigCodec, XY-Tokenizer, X-Codec2 are absent from the low-bitrate comparison), and training data scale/composition differs substantially across baselines (some trained on far less data), which is only partially addressed via a single small-scale ablation of SAC itself rather than equalized comparisons.
The code/model release link referenced in the abstract is not actually provided in the visible text, leaving full reproducibility unverified from the paper alone.

The subjective MOS study is relatively small (20 raters, 30 utterances) and limited to low-bitrate settings, and no significance testing or confidence intervals are reported for any of the reconstruction or downstream metrics, making it hard to assess whether reported gains are robust versus within typical evaluation noise.

The downstream TTS validation uses only a single relatively small backbone (Qwen3-0.6B) and a single token-rate variant (37.5 Hz), with the higher-rate (62.5 Hz) variant explicitly left unevaluated in generative settings, limiting how strongly the 'single-stage AR TTS clearly outperforms SOTA' claim generalizes.

The generalizability limitation (acknowledged by the authors) that the semantic tokenizer is ASR/text-aligned restricts applicability beyond speech (e.g., no validation on paralinguistic-heavy or multi-speaker overlapping scenarios beyond what ARCH covers) is a real scope constraint on the broader claims of the abstract about 'semantically rich representations' more generally.
